concepts.title: What Fine-Tuning Actually Changes
concepts.description: Prompting and RAG change what a frozen model conditions on for a single call; fine-tuning runs real gradient descent and permanently rewrites the model's weights -- a mechanically different, more powerful, and riskier operation than either.
learningObjectives: Explain, at the level of weight updates, what happens during a fine-tuning training step versus what happens when you add instructions or retrieved text to a prompt.

Distinguish in-context learning (transient, no weight change) from parametric learning via fine-tuning (persistent weight change), and explain why only the latter survives once a conversation or session ends.

Describe the fine-tuning training loop conceptually: loss computed against target completions, gradients computed with respect to every trainable weight, and an optimizer nudging weights to reduce that loss.
Explain catastrophic forgetting and why updating weights to improve one narrow behavior can silently degrade unrelated capabilities.
Predict, given a described training setup, whether a fine-tune is likely to improve a target behavior cleanly or put unrelated capabilities at risk.

sections.heading: In-Context Learning vs Parametric Learning
sections.body:
Every technique covered in the previous module -- a more specific instruction, a few-shot example, a retrieved document -- works by changing what gets fed into a model whose weights never move. The model reads a different sequence of tokens on each call, its internal activations shift accordingly for that one forward pass, and the output changes as a result -- but the actual numbers stored in its weight matrices are exactly the same before and after the call. This is usually called **in-context learning**: the model appears to 'learn' something from the examples or instructions in the prompt, but that appearance is entirely a property of conditioning a fixed, frozen function on a specific input. The moment that prompt is gone -- the next call doesn't include it, the session ends, someone forgets to pass the system message -- the effect is gone with it, instantly and completely, because nothing about the model itself was ever touched.

Fine-tuning is a fundamentally different operation: it is additional training, meaning it actually runs the gradient-descent procedure that originally produced the model's weights, just on a new, smaller, purpose-built dataset. The result is a model whose weight matrices literally contain different numbers than they did before -- and because those numbers are what the model consults on every single future call, whatever behavior shift the fine-tuning produced persists on every subsequent call, with no need to re-supply an instruction or an example ever again. This is the core distinction worth internalizing before anything else in this module: prompting and RAG operate on a frozen function's input; fine-tuning operates on the function itself.

sections.heading: What a Fine-Tuning Step Actually Computes
sections.body:
Recall the autoregressive generation loop from the how-LLMs-work module: a forward pass produces one logit per vocabulary entry at each position, softmax converts those into a probability distribution, and a token is selected. A fine-tuning training step reuses that exact same forward-pass machinery, but for a different purpose and with extra steps attached to it.

Given a training example -- an input plus a desired target completion -- the model runs the same forward pass it would for ordinary generation, producing a probability distribution over the vocabulary at every position in the target. Instead of sampling a token from that distribution, training computes a **loss**: a single number (typically cross-entropy loss) measuring how far the model's predicted distribution was from the actual target token at each position, averaged over the example. A low loss means the model already assigned high probability to the correct target tokens; a high loss means it assigned that probability to something else.

```python
# Conceptual shape of ONE fine-tuning training step (not real framework code)
logits = model.forward(input_tokens)                 # same forward pass as inference
loss = cross_entropy(logits, target_tokens)           # how wrong were the predictions?
loss.backward()                                        # compute d(loss)/d(weight) for EVERY weight
optimizer.step()                                       # nudge every weight slightly to reduce loss
optimizer.zero_grad()                                  # clear gradients before the next example/batch
```

The crucial extra machinery, absent entirely from inference, is `loss.backward()` and `optimizer.step()`. Backpropagation computes the gradient of the loss with respect to every single trainable weight in the model -- a partial derivative answering 'if I nudged this one weight up slightly, would the loss go up or down, and by how much?' -- for every weight, all at once. The optimizer (commonly a variant of Adam) then actually moves each weight a small step in the direction that reduces the loss. Repeat this over many examples, in batches, across multiple passes (**epochs**) through the training dataset, and the accumulated small nudges are what constitute 'the model learned something new.' Nothing here is symbolic or rule-based -- it is the identical numerical optimization process, applied to a small, targeted dataset, that produced the base model's weights in the first place, just starting from an already-trained starting point instead of from scratch.

sections.heading: Persistence, and the Real Cost of Getting It Wrong: Catastrophic Forgetting
sections.body:
Because fine-tuning writes new values into weights that are shared across every capability the model has -- not into some isolated, task-specific module -- there's no structural guarantee that improving performance on your narrow training data leaves everything else untouched. Every weight the optimizer nudges to make the target behavior more probable is also a weight that previously contributed, in some diffuse way, to dozens of other behaviors the base model was good at. Push those weights hard enough in service of a narrow objective -- too high a learning rate, too many epochs, a training set that's small or skewed relative to the full range of things the model used to do well -- and you can measurably degrade unrelated capabilities the model had before, a phenomenon called **catastrophic forgetting**.

This is genuinely dangerous specifically because it's silent by default: nothing about the fine-tuning process throws an error or a warning when it happens. Training loss on your target dataset will look great -- it's actively being optimized to go down -- while performance on tasks you never tested quietly gets worse, and the only way to notice is to have actually gone and tested those other tasks, deliberately, before and after. A model fine-tuned intensively on customer-service refund replies might become excellent at refund replies and simultaneously, invisibly, become measurably worse at general reasoning, code help, or even other customer-service categories it used to handle fine -- not because anyone told it to forget those things, but because the same shared weights that used to support them were repeatedly nudged in service of a different, narrower objective.

sections.heading: Why You Always Keep the Base Model Around, and Evaluate Broadly
sections.body:
Because forgetting is a real, silent risk rather than a rare edge case, responsible fine-tuning practice treats a candidate fine-tune the way you'd treat any risky code change: compare it against a baseline on a broad regression suite, not just the metric you were trying to improve. The base (pre-fine-tune) model is always kept available as that baseline -- a 'fine-tuned model,' mechanically, is base weights plus a set of updates, and having the unmodified original to diff behavior against is what actually lets you detect forgetting rather than assume it away.

```python
# A minimal before/after regression check -- not just the target task
baseline_scores = evaluate(base_model, eval_suite)          # covers MANY tasks, not just the target one
candidate_scores = evaluate(finetuned_model, eval_suite)

for task in eval_suite.tasks:
    delta = candidate_scores[task] - baseline_scores[task]
    if task == "target_task" and delta <= 0:
        print(f"WARNING: fine-tune did not improve the task it was meant to improve: {task}")
    if task != "target_task" and delta < -0.05:   # a real, meaningful regression threshold
        print(f"WARNING: possible forgetting on unrelated task: {task} (delta={delta:.3f})")
```

The common mistake here is gating a fine-tune's deployment purely on whether it improved the one metric it was trained for, and never checking anything else -- that check will always look successful, since the training process was directly optimizing exactly that number, while telling you nothing about whatever else might have quietly regressed alongside it.

examples.title: A Toy Fine-Tuning Step, Made Explicit
examples.code:
import torch

# A single, real (if tiny) fine-tuning step using a PyTorch-style API.
input_ids = tokenizer("Summarize: The meeting is moved to 3pm.", return_tensors="pt").input_ids
target_ids = tokenizer("The meeting time changed to 3pm.", return_tensors="pt").input_ids

optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=1e-5)

outputs = model(input_ids=input_ids, labels=target_ids)   # forward pass + built-in loss computation
loss = outputs.loss
print("loss before step:", loss.item())

loss.backward()        # gradients for every trainable weight
optimizer.step()       # every weight nudged slightly toward lower loss on THIS example
optimizer.zero_grad()  # reset for the next example

# Running this same input through the model again immediately afterward would
# typically show a LOWER loss -- the weights genuinely changed, even if by a tiny amount.
examples.explanation: This is one single step out of what a real fine-tuning run repeats many thousands of times across a whole training dataset. `model(input_ids=input_ids, labels=target_ids)` runs the same forward pass used for ordinary generation, but because `labels` is supplied, it also computes cross-entropy loss against the target tokens internally. `loss.backward()` is where the actual learning happens -- it walks the computational graph backward and computes, for every trainable weight in the entire model, how much that specific weight contributed to this particular loss value. `optimizer.step()` then applies a small, calculated nudge to every one of those weights. None of this exists in a normal inference call -- inference only ever runs the forward pass and reads off a distribution; it never computes a loss, never calls `.backward()`, and never touches the optimizer, which is exactly why running inference a thousand times never changes the model at all, while running this training step a thousand times does.

examples.title: Same Target Behavior, Two Different Mechanisms, Two Different Failure Modes
examples.explanation: Both functions can produce equally formal-sounding replies today. The difference only shows up under a very ordinary kind of production accident: a code path that builds the messages list without including the system prompt -- a refactor that drops it, a new caller of the underlying chat function that forgets it, a fallback path triggered during an outage. Approach A's formality disappears instantly and completely the moment that system message is missing, because the frozen base model has no memory of ever being asked to be formal outside of that specific input. Approach B is entirely unaffected by that same class of bug, because the formal-tone behavior isn't stored in any prompt at all -- it's stored in the weights themselves, and the weights are present on every single call regardless of what messages list gets built around them. This is the practical, production-relevant face of 'in-context learning is transient, fine-tuning is persistent': it determines which class of bugs can silently break a given behavior, and which can't.

examples.title: Catastrophic Forgetting Showing Up in an Eval Table
examples.explanation: This is the shape of a fine-tune that overfit on a narrow dataset: it was trained heavily (too many epochs, too high a learning rate, or too narrow a dataset relative to the model's full range of prior behavior) on refund-reply examples specifically, and the refund-reply metric genuinely, substantially improved -- the training process was directly optimizing for exactly that. But every one of the other three metrics, covering unrelated or only loosely related capabilities, regressed, some severely. Nothing about the training process 'chose' to sacrifice general QA or code help -- there's no mechanism in gradient descent that protects capabilities the current batch of training examples isn't reinforcing. If a team only measured `refund_reply_quality` before deploying, this fine-tune would look like an unambiguous win right up until users started noticing the model got noticeably worse at everything else it used to handle.

misconceptions.description: Fine-tuning is basically just a way to give the model a permanent, extra-long system prompt so you don't have to keep repeating the same instructions on every call.
misconceptions.clarification: The end-user-visible effect can look similar, but the mechanism is completely different, and that difference has real consequences. A system prompt is text the frozen model conditions on for one call; fine-tuning runs actual gradient descent that changes the numbers stored in the model's weights. The prompting version costs tokens on every call and vanishes instantly if that prompt is ever omitted; the fine-tuned version costs nothing extra per call and persists with no prompt at all, but carries a risk prompting never does -- catastrophic forgetting of unrelated capabilities, because the same shared weights that encode the new behavior also encode everything else the model used to do.

misconceptions.description: If a fine-tune measurably improves accuracy on the target task, it's a pure win -- there's no meaningful downside to worry about as long as that one number went up.
misconceptions.clarification: Training loss and target-task accuracy going up are exactly what the training process was directly optimizing for, so they will very reliably look good -- that tells you nothing about capabilities the training data wasn't reinforcing. Catastrophic forgetting is silent: it doesn't throw an error, and it won't show up unless you specifically evaluate a broad regression suite covering tasks unrelated to the fine-tune, comparing against the pre-fine-tune baseline model. Judging a fine-tune solely by the metric it was trained to improve is the single most common way teams ship a regression without noticing until users report it.

exercises.prompt: A team fine-tunes a general-purpose assistant model using only examples of refund-request replies, for many epochs, at a relatively high learning rate, and evaluates ONLY on a held-out set of refund-reply examples before deciding to deploy. Predict what an evaluation on unrelated tasks (general Q&A, code help) would most likely show, and explain why, even though nobody trained the model to get worse at those things.
exercises.code:
training_data = load_examples("refund_replies_only.jsonl")   # ~2,000 examples, one narrow category
finetune(base_model="assistant-v2", data=training_data, epochs=8, learning_rate=5e-4)
# deployed after refund_reply_eval_score improved from 0.61 to 0.93
hints: The training data reinforces exactly one narrow behavior, for many epochs, at a fairly aggressive learning rate -- what does that combination tend to do to weights that also support OTHER capabilities?

Nothing in gradient descent protects capabilities that the current training batch isn't reinforcing -- shared weights get nudged toward whatever the loss function is currently rewarding, regardless of what else depended on their previous values.
Consider what would actually have to be true for unrelated capabilities to be UNAFFECTED -- would that require something special to have been included in this training run? Was it?
exercises.expectedAnswer: Unrelated task performance (general Q&A, code help) is likely to have regressed measurably, even though nobody deliberately trained the model to be worse at them -- this is catastrophic forgetting, driven by training only on a narrow, single-category dataset for many epochs at a high learning rate, with no mechanism protecting the weights that supported unrelated capabilities.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Training exclusively on refund-reply examples, for many epochs, at a relatively high learning rate is close to a worst-case recipe for forgetting: many epochs means the same narrow pattern is reinforced repeatedly rather than lightly; a high learning rate means each nudge to the shared weights is larger; and a single-category dataset means nothing in the training signal ever reinforces or protects the model's other capabilities during this process. Since the model's capabilities all live in the same shared weights, repeatedly pushing those weights hard in service of one narrow objective is exactly the setup that degrades unrelated ones -- not through any explicit instruction to forget, but as a direct side effect of optimizing shared parameters toward a narrow target. The team's own evaluation never would have revealed this, because they only measured the refund-reply metric the training process was already directly optimizing -- which is precisely why a broad, pre-existing regression suite covering unrelated tasks, run before and after, is necessary to catch this kind of damage before it reaches production.

exercises.prompt: This deployment gate is meant to prevent bad fine-tunes from reaching production automatically, but after several fine-tuning rounds, users start reporting the assistant has gotten noticeably worse at tasks unrelated to what was being improved. Find the bug in the gating logic and fix it.
hints: This function only ever looks at one key, "target_task", out of what are presumably several keys in both score dictionaries -- what happens to every OTHER task's score, good or bad?

A fine-tune that improves the target task while quietly regressing several unrelated tasks would make this function return True every single time -- is that the deployment policy the team actually wants?
Fix it so deployment also requires that no unrelated task has regressed beyond some acceptable tolerance, not just that the target task improved.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original gate checks exactly one number -- whether the target task improved -- and ignores every other entry in `baseline_scores` and `candidate_scores` entirely, even though those dicts clearly contain scores for other tasks too (that's the whole reason they're passed in as multi-key dicts rather than single floats). Since a narrow fine-tune reliably improves its own target metric while sometimes silently regressing unrelated ones, this gate would happily approve exactly the kind of fine-tune that caused the reported problem: forgetting on unrelated tasks. The fix keeps the original requirement (the target task must actually improve) but adds a second requirement -- loop over every other task in the eval suite and block deployment if any of them regressed by more than an explicit, chosen tolerance relative to the baseline. This doesn't eliminate forgetting, but it stops a forgetting-heavy fine-tune from being auto-approved just because its own target metric happened to look good.

assessments.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes what fine-tuning changes from what prompting and RAG change?
options: Fine-tuning only changes the default system prompt that gets prepended to every call; prompting and RAG change the model's weights.

Fine-tuning runs gradient descent that updates the model's weights, persisting after the training run ends; prompting and RAG leave the weights untouched and only change what a frozen model conditions on for one specific call.
RAG updates the model's weights to memorize retrieved documents, while fine-tuning and prompting only affect the current call.
There is no real difference -- all three are different ways of writing instructions the model reads before responding.
assessments.explanation: Fine-tuning is additional training: it computes gradients and updates weights via an optimizer, and those updated weights persist across every future call with no need to repeat anything. Prompting and RAG never touch the model's weights at all -- they only change the input a fixed, frozen model conditions on for that one call, and the effect vanishes the instant that input isn't included again. Option A and C both invert which technique changes weights. Option D collapses a mechanically real distinction (weight updates that persist vs. per-call conditioning that doesn't) into 'it's all just instructions,' which is exactly the misconception this concept is meant to correct.

assessments.prompt: A senior engineer proposes: 'We don't need a retrieval system anymore -- let's just fine-tune the model on a fresh snapshot of our documentation every week, so it always knows the latest information.' Explain, mechanically, why weekly fine-tuning is a fundamentally different (and riskier) way to keep a model current than a retrieval system that leaves weights frozen, and identify a specific risk beyond staleness that this weekly-retraining plan introduces.
assessments.modelAnswer: A retrieval system never touches the model's weights at all -- it keeps the generation model completely frozen and simply changes what text is included in the prompt for a given call, by searching an index that can itself be updated in minutes whenever the underlying documentation changes. Fine-tuning is a categorically different operation: it runs real gradient descent, computing a loss against target completions and nudging every trainable weight to reduce that loss, which is slow, computationally expensive, and -- critically -- changes the model itself rather than just its input. Doing that every week doesn't just inherit the ordinary problems of fine-tuning for knowledge (weights encode facts diffusely rather than storing them verbatim, so even a fresh fine-tune isn't a reliable, exact lookup the way injecting retrieved text into a prompt is); it compounds a second, distinct risk across every retraining cycle: catastrophic forgetting. Each week's fine-tuning run nudges shared weights toward that week's documentation snapshot, with no guarantee that doing so leaves every previously-learned capability, including whatever the *previous* week's fine-tune reinforced, fully intact. Run this weekly for months and you have months of accumulated, uncontrolled weight drift, with no single point where anyone deliberately verified that some earlier capability hasn't quietly degraded along the way -- unlike a retrieval index, which can be corrected, rolled back, or inspected for exactly what text it will inject, with zero risk to the underlying model's other behaviors, because the model itself never changes.

assessments.prompt: During an ordinary inference call to a model, which of the operations involved in a fine-tuning training step are actually performed?
options: Only the forward pass -- logits are computed and a token is selected from the resulting distribution; no loss is computed, and no backward pass or optimizer step ever runs.
The forward pass and loss computation both run, but the backward pass and optimizer step are skipped.
The forward pass, loss computation, and backward pass all run, but the optimizer step is skipped to save time.
All four steps -- forward pass, loss computation, backward pass, and optimizer step -- run on every inference call, just using a very small learning rate.
assessments.explanation: Inference only ever runs the forward pass and reads off a probability distribution to select a token from -- there is no target completion to compute a loss against, so nothing analogous to `loss.backward()` or `optimizer.step()` ever executes, which is exactly why running inference many times never changes the model's weights at all. Options B, C, and D all incorrectly assume some piece of the training-specific machinery runs during ordinary inference, when none of it does -- loss computation, gradients, and optimizer updates are exclusively part of a training step, never part of a generation call.

assessments.prompt: Per this module, why is catastrophic forgetting described as 'silent by default'?
options: Because it only ever affects models that are deployed without any monitoring dashboard configured.

Because training loss on the target dataset keeps looking good -- it's the exact metric being directly optimized -- while performance on unrelated, untested capabilities can degrade with no error, warning, or signal from the training process itself; it's only detected by deliberately evaluating those other capabilities before and after.
Because forgetting only ever happens during the very first epoch of training, before most logging frameworks are typically initialized.
Because catastrophic forgetting always throws a specific, named exception that many teams accidentally catch and silently swallow in their training scripts.
assessments.explanation: The module is explicit that nothing about the fine-tuning process throws an error or warning when forgetting happens -- the target metric being trained for will reliably look good since it's exactly what's being optimized, while unrelated capabilities can quietly degrade, detectable only through deliberate evaluation of tasks outside the training objective. Option A, C, and D all invent specific mechanisms or triggers -- missing dashboards, a first-epoch-only timing, a swallowed exception -- that the module never describes; the actual reason is simply that nothing in the training loop checks or reports on capabilities it isn't currently optimizing for.

assessments.prompt: Per this module, what's the specific flaw in gating a fine-tune's deployment purely on whether it improved the one metric it was trained for?
options: There's no real flaw -- if the target metric improved, that alone is sufficient evidence the fine-tune is safe to ship.

The target metric will reliably look good precisely because the training process was directly optimizing exactly that number, while telling you nothing about whether unrelated capabilities silently regressed -- only a broader before/after evaluation across other tasks, against the retained base-model baseline, can reveal that.
The flaw is that target-metric evaluation is always less accurate than LLM-as-judge evaluation, regardless of what specific capability is being measured.
The flaw is that target-metric-only gating requires re-running the full training job twice, which needlessly doubles compute cost without any real benefit.
assessments.explanation: The module explicitly calls out this exact mistake: gating deployment on the trained-for metric alone will always look successful, since that's precisely what the optimization was targeting, while providing zero visibility into whatever else might have quietly regressed -- which is why a broad regression suite compared against the retained base-model baseline is the recommended practice instead. Option A directly contradicts the module's core warning. Option C introduces an unrelated and unsupported comparison to LLM-as-judge evaluation. Option D misdiagnoses the issue as a compute-cost problem rather than a blind-spot-in-measurement problem.

concepts.title: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning and LoRA
concepts.description: Full fine-tuning has to store gradients and optimizer state for every one of a model's parameters; LoRA gets most of the practical benefit of fine-tuning by freezing the original weights entirely and training a tiny, low-rank update alongside them instead -- which is also why adapters can be swapped like plug-ins.
learningObjectives: Explain why full fine-tuning of a large model is memory- and compute-intensive independent of how much training data you have, in terms of gradients and optimizer state per parameter.
Explain the core LoRA idea: freezing the original weight matrices and learning a small low-rank update matrix pair alongside them.
Explain what rank controls in LoRA and the practical tradeoff between rank, learning capacity, and resource cost.
Explain why LoRA adapters are small, swappable, and composable in ways full fine-tuned weight copies are not.
Identify when full fine-tuning is still worth its extra cost over a parameter-efficient approach, and when it clearly isn't.

sections.heading: The Memory Wall of Full Fine-Tuning
sections.body:
Running a large model for inference only needs to hold its weights (and, briefly, its activations) in memory. Training that same model needs considerably more, because gradient descent has to remember more than just the current weight values. For every single trainable parameter, a full fine-tuning run typically needs: the weight itself, the gradient of the loss with respect to that weight (computed fresh on every step), and -- if using a modern optimizer like Adam or AdamW, which is almost universal -- two additional running-average tensors per parameter (commonly called the first and second moment) that the optimizer uses to adapt its step size per parameter over time.

Add those up and full fine-tuning with Adam-family optimizers needs roughly four times the raw parameter memory at minimum (weights, gradients, and two optimizer moments), on top of the activation memory needed for the forward and backward passes -- before you've even loaded a single training example. For a model with tens of billions of parameters, this pushes full fine-tuning out of reach of anything but serious multi-GPU infrastructure, and it does so regardless of whether your actual training dataset is 500 examples or 500,000 -- the memory cost is a function of model size, not dataset size. This is the concrete, mechanical reason teams look for a cheaper way to adapt a model than updating every single one of its weights.

sections.heading: The Core LoRA Idea: Freeze the Big Matrix, Learn a Small Update
sections.body:
**LoRA** (Low-Rank Adaptation) sidesteps the memory wall with a specific, elegant trick: instead of updating a weight matrix W directly, LoRA leaves W completely frozen -- untouched, no gradients computed for it at all -- and instead learns a separate, additive update expressed as the product of two much smaller matrices. If W has shape (d x k), LoRA introduces a matrix A of shape (d x r) and a matrix B of shape (r x k), where r -- the **rank** -- is a small number, often somewhere between 8 and 64, chosen to be tiny relative to d and k. Only A and B are trained; at inference, the effective weight used is `W + (A @ B) * scaling`, but W itself, the large original matrix, is exactly what it always was.

```python
# Conceptual shapes: original weight matrix vs its LoRA adapter
d, k, r = 4096, 4096, 8

full_matrix_params = d * k                      # 16,777,216 trainable params, if fine-tuned fully
lora_params = (d * r) + (r * k)                  # A: 4096x8, B: 8x4096
print(full_matrix_params, lora_params)           # 16,777,216  vs  65,536
print(full_matrix_params / lora_params)          # roughly 256x fewer trainable parameters for this matrix
```

The hypothesis this rests on -- and one that's held up well empirically across a wide range of models and tasks -- is that the *change* a pretrained model needs to adapt to a new, comparatively narrow task or style genuinely lives in a low-dimensional subspace, even though the model's full weight space is enormous. You don't need the full expressive power of a (4096 x 4096) update to teach a model a consistent tone shift or a narrow classification boundary; a much lower-rank approximation of that update captures nearly all the useful adaptation, at a tiny fraction of the trainable-parameter count -- and since only A and B need gradients and optimizer state, the memory wall from full fine-tuning mostly disappears.

sections.heading: Why Rank Is the Knob That Actually Matters
sections.body:
Rank (r) is the single most consequential hyperparameter in a LoRA setup, and it's worth being precise about what it trades off. A **rank too low** for the behavior shift you're actually asking for can genuinely underfit -- if the needed adaptation really does require more expressive capacity than a very low-rank matrix product can represent, training will plateau at a worse result than a higher rank would reach, no matter how much training data or how many epochs you throw at it. A **rank too high**, on the other hand, starts eating back the exact advantages LoRA exists to provide: more trainable parameters, more memory and compute, slower training, and -- because a large enough rank starts to approximate full fine-tuning -- a growing exposure to the same catastrophic-forgetting risk covered in the previous concept, since a higher-capacity update has more room to overfit narrowly on the training set at the expense of everything else.

In practice, teams don't apply LoRA to literally every weight matrix in a model either -- it's commonly applied to a subset, often the attention projection matrices, leaving many other weight matrices frozen and untouched entirely, on the empirical finding that adapting a subset of layers already captures most of the useful behavior shift. Both the rank and which layers to adapt are usually chosen empirically, by trying a few settings and measuring actual task performance, rather than derived from a fixed formula -- there's no rank that's correct for every task, only a rank that turns out to be enough for the specific adaptation you're trying to make.

sections.heading: Swappable, Composable Adapters
sections.body:
Because the original weights are never modified, what a LoRA fine-tuning run actually produces is small: just the trained A and B matrices for whichever layers were adapted, typically megabytes rather than the gigabytes a full copy of the model's weights would require. This has a very practical consequence for how fine-tuned behavior gets served in production: a single base model can be loaded once, and many different LoRA adapters -- one per customer, one per task, one per style -- can be kept on hand as small files and swapped in (added to the frozen base weights) depending on which request is being served, without ever reloading the (large, slow-to-load) base model itself.

```python
# One shared base model, many small swappable adapters
base_model = load_base_model("assistant-70b")

def generate_for_customer(customer_id, prompt, adapter_paths):
    base_model.set_active_adapter(adapter_paths[customer_id])   # loads a small A/B matrix pair
    return base_model.generate(prompt)
```

Contrast this with full fine-tuning, where each fine-tuned variant is an entirely separate copy of every single weight in the model -- serving many full fine-tuned variants means storing and potentially loading many full-size copies of a very large model, which is expensive in a way that swapping small adapters simply isn't. This is precisely what makes it commercially and operationally feasible to offer many customers their own 'custom' fine-tuned behavior without provisioning a separate full model deployment for each one.

sections.heading: When Full Fine-Tuning Still Wins
sections.body: LoRA and other parameter-efficient methods are the sensible default starting point given how much cheaper and lower-risk they are, but they aren't a universal replacement for full fine-tuning. If the capability shift you actually need is large -- genuinely new domain knowledge or behavior far outside what the base model's existing representations support, rather than a narrower adaptation of skills it already mostly has -- a low-rank update may simply lack the expressive capacity to represent the needed change well, no matter how it's tuned, because the underlying assumption (that the needed update lies in a low-dimensional subspace) stops holding as the required shift gets larger and more fundamental. In those cases, full fine-tuning (or, at the extreme end, further pretraining on a large new corpus) remains the appropriate, if more expensive and riskier, tool. The practical decision process mirrors the fine-tuning-vs-RAG-vs-prompting heuristic from the earlier module: start with the cheapest, lowest-risk option that could plausibly work -- here, a modest-rank LoRA adapter -- and only escalate to the more expensive, higher-capacity option once you have concrete evidence the cheaper one is falling short, rather than assuming the most powerful available tool is automatically the right first choice.

examples.title: Rough Trainable-Parameter Counts: Full Fine-Tuning vs LoRA
examples.code:
def full_finetune_trainable_params(total_model_params):
    return total_model_params   # every weight is trainable

def lora_trainable_params(d, k, r, num_adapted_matrices):
    per_matrix = (d * r) + (r * k)
    return per_matrix * num_adapted_matrices

total_model_params = 7_000_000_000   # a 7B-parameter model
lora_params = lora_trainable_params(d=4096, k=4096, r=16, num_adapted_matrices=64)

print(full_finetune_trainable_params(total_model_params))   # 7,000,000,000
print(lora_params)                                            # 8,388,608
print(total_model_params / lora_params)                       # roughly 834x fewer trainable parameters
examples.explanation: The full fine-tuning figure is trivial -- every single weight in the model is trainable, so the trainable-parameter count IS the model's total parameter count, with all the gradient and optimizer-state memory that implies for every single one of those seven billion numbers. The LoRA figure only counts the small A and B matrices actually being trained across the (here, illustrative) 64 adapted weight matrices, at rank 16 -- roughly 800 times fewer trainable parameters for a model of this size. This gap is precisely why LoRA fine-tuning is often practical on hardware that couldn't remotely hold the optimizer state required for full fine-tuning of the same base model -- the frozen base weights still need to be loaded for the forward pass, but no gradients or optimizer moments need to be stored for any of them, only for the comparatively tiny adapter matrices.

examples.title: A LoRA Update as Matrix Math
examples.code:
import numpy as np

# A small, illustrative frozen weight matrix (imagine this is a real, much larger,
# pretrained weight matrix inside a transformer layer)
W = np.random.randn(6, 6)

# LoRA adapter: rank r=2, much smaller than the 6x6 original
r = 2
A = np.random.randn(6, r) * 0.01   # trained
B = np.random.randn(r, 6) * 0.01   # trained
scaling = 1.0

W_effective = W + scaling * (A @ B)   # used at inference; W itself never changes

print("Original W shape:", W.shape)             # (6, 6) -- 36 values, frozen
print("A shape, B shape:", A.shape, B.shape)      # (6, 2), (2, 6) -- 12 + 12 = 24 trainable values
print("A @ B shape:", (A @ B).shape)              # (6, 6) -- matches W's shape, so it can be added directly
examples.explanation: `A @ B` produces a matrix the same shape as `W`, even though `A` and `B` individually are much smaller -- this is the entire mechanical trick behind LoRA: the low-rank product of two thin matrices can be added directly to the original weight matrix because matrix multiplication of a (d x r) matrix by an (r x k) matrix always produces a (d x k) result, matching the shape of whatever full-size matrix it's meant to adjust. `W` is never assigned to or modified anywhere in this code -- only `A` and `B` would receive gradients during actual training, and `W_effective` is computed fresh at inference time by combining the frozen original with the trained low-rank update. In this tiny toy example the parameter savings look modest (24 vs 36), but the ratio grows enormous for the kind of matrix sizes real transformer layers actually use, which is exactly what the previous example demonstrated at realistic scale.

examples.title: Swapping Adapters Per Request
examples.explanation: The expensive, slow part -- loading a 70-billion-parameter base model -- happens exactly once, in `__init__`. Every subsequent call only swaps in a small adapter file if the requested customer differs from whichever adapter is currently active, which is a cheap operation compared to loading an entirely different full-size model. This is what makes serving many distinct 'custom fine-tuned' behaviors, one per customer, operationally realistic: the cost that scales with the number of customers is the small, cheap adapter-swap cost, not the enormous, expensive base-model-load cost, which is paid only once regardless of how many customers or adapters exist. Note the explicit check against `self._active_adapter_id` -- without it, this code would risk exactly the bug explored in the debugging exercise below, where a stale, previously-loaded adapter keeps getting used for the wrong customer.

misconceptions.description: LoRA fine-tunes the whole model, just in a faster, more memory-efficient way.
misconceptions.clarification: LoRA does not train the model's original weight matrices at all -- it freezes them completely and trains only a separate, much smaller pair of low-rank matrices that get added to the frozen weights at inference time. The base model's own weights, numerically, never change during a LoRA fine-tuning run. This is precisely why a single base model deployment can serve many different LoRA adapters interchangeably: the shared, frozen part is identical across all of them, and only the small adapter differs.

misconceptions.description: A higher LoRA rank is always strictly better, since it gives the adapter more capacity to learn the target behavior.
misconceptions.clarification: Higher rank does increase capacity, but capacity beyond what the target adaptation actually needs doesn't sit idle -- it costs more memory and compute to train, moves the setup closer to full fine-tuning's forgetting risk, and gives the optimizer more room to overfit narrowly to the training set's quirks rather than the intended general behavior. Since the practical premise behind LoRA is that most useful adaptations genuinely fit in a fairly low-rank subspace, an unnecessarily high rank usually buys little or no additional quality while giving back a real fraction of LoRA's core advantages over full fine-tuning.

exercises.prompt: Write two functions: full_param_count(d, k) returning the number of trainable parameters if a (d x k) weight matrix were fully fine-tuned, and lora_param_count(d, k, r) returning the number of trainable parameters for a LoRA adapter of rank r applied to that same matrix. Then write savings_ratio(d, k, r) that returns how many times fewer trainable parameters the LoRA adapter uses compared to full fine-tuning of that matrix.
hints: A fully fine-tuned (d x k) matrix has exactly d * k trainable parameters -- every entry in the matrix.
A LoRA adapter introduces two matrices: A of shape (d x r) and B of shape (r x k). Its trainable parameter count is the sum of both matrices' sizes.
savings_ratio should just divide the two counts you already computed -- avoid duplicating the arithmetic, call the two functions you already wrote.
exercises.solutionExplanation: `full_param_count` is simply the size of the full matrix, since every entry would receive its own gradient and optimizer state under full fine-tuning. `lora_param_count` reflects LoRA's actual added structure: matrix A contributes d*r trainable values and matrix B contributes r*k trainable values, and since A and B are the ONLY trainable parameters for this weight (the original d*k matrix stays frozen), their sum is the adapter's full trainable-parameter count. `savings_ratio` reuses both previous functions rather than recomputing the arithmetic, which keeps the relationship between the three functions explicit: it directly answers 'how many times fewer trainable parameters does the LoRA version need,' which is exactly the number that determines how much of the full-fine-tuning memory wall a given rank choice actually avoids.

exercises.prompt: This multi-tenant serving function is supposed to respond to each customer using that customer's own fine-tuned LoRA adapter. Instead, every customer after the first one gets responses generated using the FIRST customer's adapter, regardless of their own customer_id. Find and fix the bug.
hints: The adapter is only ever loaded once, guarded by the `_adapter_loaded` flag -- which customer_id was active the very first time this function ran?
Every call after the first one skips the `if` block entirely, since the flag is already set to True and never gets reset or re-checked against the CURRENT customer_id.
The fix needs to track WHICH adapter is currently active, and reload whenever the requested customer differs from that -- not just whether any adapter has EVER been loaded.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original guard, `_adapter_loaded`, is a plain boolean that only ever records 'has an adapter been loaded at least once,' not 'which customer's adapter is currently active.' Once the very first request sets it to True, every subsequent request -- regardless of a completely different `customer_id` -- skips the adapter-loading branch entirely and silently keeps using whatever adapter happened to load first, generating every future customer's response with the wrong customer's fine-tuned behavior. The fix replaces the boolean with a stored `_active_customer` value and compares it against the current request's `customer_id`, reloading the adapter specifically when they differ. This mirrors a completely ordinary shared-mutable-state bug -- the fix is conceptually the same as correctly invalidating any cache when its key changes, just applied to which small adapter file is currently merged onto the shared base model.

assessments.prompt: In a LoRA fine-tuning setup, what happens to the model's original weight matrices, and what actually gets trained?
options: The original weight matrices are trained at a lower numerical precision to save memory; nothing new is added to the model.
The original weight matrices are frozen and never updated; a separate, much smaller pair of low-rank matrices is trained and added to them at inference time.
The original weight matrices are trained normally; LoRA only changes how the tokenizer processes input to save memory.
The original weight matrices are deleted and replaced entirely by the low-rank matrices, which become the new model.
assessments.explanation: LoRA's entire mechanism rests on freezing the original weight matrices completely -- no gradients are computed for them, and their values never change -- while training a separate, additive low-rank update (the product of two small matrices, A and B) alongside them. Option A describes quantization, a different and unrelated memory-saving technique. Option C incorrectly claims the original weights are trained normally, which would just be full fine-tuning and defeats the entire purpose of the low-rank adapter. Option D is wrong because the original weights are never deleted or replaced -- they remain fully intact and are combined with the adapter's output at inference time, which is exactly what allows the same frozen base weights to be reused underneath many different adapters.

assessments.prompt: A teammate asks how a company can offer hundreds of enterprise customers their own 'custom fine-tuned' version of a very large model without provisioning hundreds of full copies of that model in production. Explain how LoRA-based adapters make this feasible, and specifically what does and does not get duplicated per customer.
assessments.modelAnswer: The key fact that makes this feasible is that a LoRA fine-tune never modifies the base model's own weights at all -- training only produces a separate, additive pair of small low-rank matrices (commonly called an adapter) for whichever layers were adapted, and those adapter files are typically megabytes in size rather than the many gigabytes a full copy of a large model's weights would require. What gets duplicated per customer is only that small adapter: each enterprise customer's fine-tune produces their own tiny A/B matrix pair, trained on their own data, capturing whatever narrow behavior shift is specific to them. What does NOT get duplicated is the base model itself -- the large, expensive-to-load set of original weights is loaded exactly once by the serving infrastructure and shared across every customer's requests. At request time, the system simply swaps in (adds) whichever customer's small adapter matrices onto that one shared base model before generating a response, and swaps in a different customer's adapter for the next request. This means the operational cost that scales with the number of customers is the cheap cost of storing and swapping small adapter files, not the expensive cost of storing and loading hundreds of full-size model copies -- which is precisely the cost structure that makes offering many customers their own custom behavior commercially viable in a way that would be impractical if every customer required a genuinely separate full fine-tune and a separate full model deployment.

assessments.prompt: Per this module, why does full fine-tuning with an Adam-family optimizer need roughly four times the raw parameter memory as a bare minimum, even before a single training example is loaded?
options: Because Adam-family optimizers require four separate full copies of the training dataset to be held in memory simultaneously.

Because for every trainable parameter, memory must hold the weight itself, its gradient, and two optimizer moment tensors that Adam-family optimizers use to adapt step size per parameter -- four values per parameter at minimum, before activation memory is even counted.
Because the forward pass must be run four separate times per training example to compute a numerically stable loss estimate.
Because tokenizing text for training requires four times more memory than tokenizing the same text for inference.
assessments.explanation: The module breaks this down explicitly: the weight, its gradient, and two running-average optimizer moments per parameter together account for the roughly 4x figure, entirely independent of dataset size or activation memory. Option A misattributes the multiplier to dataset copies, which isn't what Adam-family optimizers store. Option C invents a repeated-forward-pass requirement the module never describes. Option D misapplies the multiplier to tokenization, an unrelated step in the pipeline.

assessments.prompt: Per this module, what's the practical risk of choosing a LoRA rank much higher than what the target adaptation actually needs?
options: A higher rank always causes training to fail outright with an out-of-memory error, regardless of the model or hardware involved.

A higher rank increases memory and compute cost, and as it grows large enough to start approximating full fine-tuning, it also increases exposure to the same catastrophic-forgetting risk covered for full fine-tuning -- often without a corresponding gain in quality.
A higher rank makes the adapter's matrix shapes incompatible with the frozen base model, so it can no longer be added to it at inference time.
A higher rank is purely beneficial with no real tradeoff, since LoRA's design guarantees that more capacity can never hurt.
assessments.explanation: The module directly names this tradeoff: rank beyond what's needed costs more memory and compute, and as it grows large enough to resemble full fine-tuning, it inherits more of full fine-tuning's forgetting risk, with a higher-capacity update having more room to overfit narrowly rather than generalize -- often for little or no additional benefit. Option A overstates the consequence as a guaranteed hard failure. Option C is incorrect -- the matrix-shape math (A is d x r, B is r x k) works for any rank r, so compatibility isn't the issue. Option D directly contradicts the module's explicit warning about rank being a real tradeoff, not a free lever.

assessments.prompt: Per this module, what specifically makes it operationally feasible to serve many customers their own custom fine-tuned behavior using LoRA, in a way that full fine-tuning would not support as cheaply?
options: LoRA adapters eliminate the need to load the base model at all, so no shared infrastructure is required for any customer.

Only the small adapter (the trained A and B matrices) differs per customer and can be swapped cheaply onto one shared, frozen base model loaded exactly once, whereas full fine-tuning would require storing and loading a separate full-size model copy per customer.
LoRA adapters automatically merge every customer's behavior into a single blended response, so only one adapter is ever needed regardless of how many customers exist.
Full fine-tuning and LoRA cost exactly the same to serve at scale; the only feasibility difference between them is in training time, not serving cost.
assessments.explanation: The module's serving example is explicit about this: the large base model is loaded once and shared, and only small, megabyte-scale adapter files differ per customer and get swapped in cheaply, in sharp contrast to full fine-tuning's requirement of a separate full-size model copy per customer. Option A is wrong -- the base model still must be loaded, just once rather than per customer. Option C invents an automatic-blending behavior the module never describes; each customer's adapter is kept and applied separately. Option D ignores the serving-cost difference the module explicitly attributes to what must be stored and loaded per customer.

concepts.title: Dataset Preparation for Fine-Tuning
concepts.description: A fine-tuning dataset's quality matters more than its raw size, because gradient descent treats every labeled example as equally trustworthy signal -- a mislabeled or unrepresentative example doesn't just fail to help, it actively teaches the model the wrong association with exactly the same confidence as a correct one.
learningObjectives: Explain why a fine-tuning dataset's format needs to exactly mirror the real inference-time request shape, and predict the consequence when it doesn't.
Explain, mechanically in terms of gradient updates, why a mislabeled training example actively pushes weights toward the wrong behavior rather than merely failing to help.
Explain the quality-over-quantity principle and why the review bar must scale with dataset size rather than staying fixed.
Identify dataset problems that survive per-example correctness checks: duplication, distribution mismatch with production traffic, and missing coverage of edge cases or minority classes.
Design a dataset preparation checklist -- deduplication, format validation, label-balance checks, and a held-out validation split -- and explain what failure mode each step catches.

sections.heading: Format Fidelity: Train the Way You'll Serve
sections.body:
A fine-tuning dataset teaches the model a mapping: 'given input shaped like this, produce output shaped like that.' That mapping is only useful if the 'input shaped like this' half genuinely matches what real production requests look like. If your training examples are built from bare user messages with no system prompt, no retrieved context, and no conversation history, but your actual production requests always include all three, the model has been trained on a distribution of inputs that doesn't match what it will actually be asked to handle -- and there's no guarantee that whatever it learned from the clean, minimal training format transfers cleanly to the messier, fuller shape of a real request.

This sounds like an obvious thing to get right, and yet it's a genuinely common failure mode precisely because training data is often assembled separately, sometimes by a different team or a different pipeline, from the code that builds real production requests -- the two can drift apart from each other silently, with nobody noticing until the fine-tuned model's behavior in production looks noticeably weaker than it did during evaluation on the training format. The practical fix is boring but effective: generate training examples using the exact same request-building code path used in production (or a faithful, actively-maintained copy of it), rather than a hand-rolled, simplified version that happens to be more convenient to construct by hand.

sections.heading: Why Bad Examples Actively Hurt, Not Just Fail to Help
sections.body:
It's tempting to think of a mislabeled or wrong training example as simply 'wasted' -- a data point that contributes nothing useful, diluting the dataset slightly but otherwise harmless, the way a blank line does nothing to a sum. That's not what actually happens. Recall from the mechanics of a training step: every example produces a gradient telling the optimizer, with a specific direction and magnitude, to nudge weights toward assigning higher probability to that example's target completion given its input. Gradient descent has no notion of 'this particular example is unreliable, weight it less' unless you explicitly build that in -- by default, every labeled example is trusted equally, and its gradient is applied with exactly the same confidence as every other example's.

So a mislabeled example -- a review that's actually negative but labeled positive, a ticket that's actually urgent but labeled routine -- doesn't sit inertly in the dataset; it actively teaches the model 'when you see input like this, the correct-sounding response looks like that,' where 'that' is wrong. If it's a one-off, isolated error among many correct examples, its individual gradient signal is small relative to the accumulated signal from everything else, and the net effect may be negligible. But if a meaningful fraction of the dataset shares a *systematic* labeling error -- the same annotator consistently mislabeling one category, an automated labeling script with a consistent bug -- that's not noise that averages out; it's a consistent, repeated signal, exactly the kind gradient descent is good at learning, just pointed at the wrong target. A dataset doesn't need to be mostly wrong to cause real damage -- a systematic, correlated error affecting even a modest fraction of examples can measurably bias the fine-tuned behavior in that error's specific direction.

sections.heading: Quality vs Quantity: Where the Tradeoff Actually Lies
sections.body:
None of this means more data is bad -- more genuinely correct, representative data is almost always better. The actual tradeoff is that more data isn't free either: it takes real time to review, it costs more compute to train on, and critically, if the review effort doesn't scale along with the added volume, growing the dataset just grows the absolute number of unreviewed, potentially-wrong examples sitting inside it, even if the *rate* of errors stays constant. Ten thousand automatically-scraped examples with an unexamined 5% error rate contain about five hundred actively-wrong training signals; a hand-reviewed set of one thousand examples with a verified near-zero error rate contains close to none.

Practical experience across many real fine-tuning projects backs this up: for a reasonably narrow, well-specified behavior shift, a few hundred to a few thousand carefully verified examples routinely outperforms tens of thousands of unreviewed ones. There's no universal number for 'enough data' -- it's genuinely task-dependent and has to be found empirically -- but the review bar has to scale with however much data you're adding; treating 'more data' and 'more review effort' as separable decisions, where you can grow one without the other, is how a dataset quietly accumulates enough bad signal to measurably hurt the fine-tune despite looking, at a glance, like an impressively large training set.

sections.heading: Coverage and Distribution Match: Clean Isn't the Same as Representative
sections.body:
A dataset can pass every individual per-example accuracy check -- every label genuinely correct, every example genuinely well-formed -- and still be a poor training set, if its overall distribution doesn't match what the model will actually encounter in production. This is exactly the same underlying problem covered for in-context few-shot examples in the prompting module (a sentiment classifier shown only positive and neutral examples has no demonstrated precedent for negative), just baked in permanently through weight updates instead of temporarily through one prompt: if your fine-tuning examples are overwhelmingly short and simple while production traffic is often long and complicated, or overwhelmingly one tone or language while production traffic is more varied, the fine-tune will reliably reproduce whatever narrow slice of behavior the training distribution demonstrated, and handle everything outside that slice with no real precedent to draw on.

The only reliable way to catch this is to hold out a validation split drawn from the *same* distribution as training (not just a random slice cut from the same possibly-skewed dataset, but ideally sampled independently from something closer to real production traffic), and measure performance on that split specifically -- because training loss alone, measured only on the training set itself, can keep decreasing even as the model increasingly just memorizes quirks specific to the training examples rather than learning behavior that generalizes to the fuller range of inputs it will actually see. A steadily dropping training loss is consistent with genuine learning and with pure memorization alike; a held-out validation set drawn from a representative distribution is what actually distinguishes the two.

sections.heading: A Practical Preparation Checklist
sections.body: Pulling the previous sections together into concrete practice: **deduplicate** near-identical examples before training, since exact or near-exact duplicates don't add new signal, they just inflate the effective weight of whatever pattern they happen to share, sometimes causing the model to overfit toward one overrepresented case at the expense of everything else. **Verify format** matches the real production request shape exactly, not a simplified hand-built approximation of it. **Human-review a genuine random sample** of the dataset -- not just the first ten examples someone happened to look at while building it, since early examples are often the most carefully constructed and least representative of what crept in later. **Check label and category balance**, and deliberately verify that minority classes and edge cases are actually represented, not just technically present in token numbers too small to matter. **Hold out a validation split** drawn from a distribution that matches real traffic, and track validation performance -- not just training loss -- across the training run. And after training completes, **re-run the broad regression evaluation** from the previous concept, since a dataset-quality problem and a catastrophic-forgetting problem can produce very similar-looking symptoms (the model getting worse at things it used to handle fine) for genuinely different underlying reasons, and distinguishing between them usually starts with going back and re-examining exactly what the training data actually contained.

examples.title: Format Mismatch Between Training Data and Real Requests
examples.explanation: The training example is a clean, bare prompt/completion pair with no system message, no retrieved context, and no conversation history -- convenient to write by hand in bulk, but nothing like what `build_production_request` actually sends to the model at inference time, which wraps the question inside a much longer structure with grounding instructions and injected context. A model fine-tuned exclusively on the bare format has been taught a mapping from a kind of input it will essentially never see in production to the desired output style -- it may still perform reasonably, since language models often generalize somewhat across superficial formatting differences, but there's no guarantee of that, and the safer, more reliable approach is generating training examples through the exact same request-construction function used in production, so the model is trained on input that genuinely matches what it will be asked to handle.

examples.title: One Systematically Mislabeled Category Among Many Correct Ones
examples.code:
dataset = [
    {"text": "Loved this, exceeded expectations!", "label": "positive"},        # correct
    {"text": "Terrible, broke after one day.", "label": "negative"},           # correct
    {"text": "It's okay, does the job.", "label": "neutral"},                  # correct
    {"text": "Waste of money, do not buy.", "label": "neutral"},               # WRONG -- actually negative
    {"text": "Completely useless, regret this purchase.", "label": "neutral"}, # WRONG -- same systematic error
    {"text": "Great value, works perfectly.", "label": "positive"},           # correct
]

# Suppose this "neutral for clearly negative" mislabeling pattern came from one
# annotator's consistent misunderstanding of the labeling guidelines, and
# affects roughly 20% of the negative-review examples across the full dataset.
examples.explanation: Only two of the six examples shown are mislabeled, and they're not random, isolated mistakes -- they share the exact same systematic error: clearly negative reviews being labeled neutral. A single isolated mislabel, surrounded by hundreds of correct examples, would contribute a small, likely-overwhelmed gradient signal. But a *systematic* pattern like this one, affecting a consistent fifth of an entire category across the full dataset, is a repeated, correlated signal -- exactly the kind of regularity gradient descent is effective at picking up on, just pointed in the wrong direction. The realistic consequence isn't that the model becomes wildly unreliable everywhere; it's that the model becomes measurably biased specifically toward under-flagging negative sentiment as neutral, in rough proportion to how strongly and how often that particular error pattern appeared in training -- a subtle, specific bias that a spot-check of the first few examples in the dataset would very likely miss entirely.

examples.title: A Dataset Validation Report Before Training
examples.code:
from collections import Counter

def validate_dataset(examples, expected_format_keys, min_label_fraction=0.05):
    report = {}

    seen_texts = [ex["prompt"] for ex in examples]
    report["duplicate_count"] = len(seen_texts) - len(set(seen_texts))

    report["malformed_examples"] = [
        i for i, ex in enumerate(examples) if not expected_format_keys.issubset(ex.keys())
    ]

    label_counts = Counter(ex.get("label") for ex in examples if "label" in ex)
    total = sum(label_counts.values())
    if total:
        report["underrepresented_labels"] = [
            label for label, count in label_counts.items()
            if (count / total) < min_label_fraction
        ]

    lengths = [len(ex["prompt"]) for ex in examples]
    report["length_range"] = (min(lengths), max(lengths)) if lengths else (0, 0)

    return report

report = validate_dataset(
    examples=dataset,
    expected_format_keys={"prompt", "completion"},
)
print(report)
examples.explanation: Each check in this report targets a specific failure mode from the explanation, not a vague notion of 'data quality.' `duplicate_count` catches near-duplicate examples that would otherwise inflate one pattern's effective weight during training. `malformed_examples` catches examples missing the fields the training format actually requires, which would otherwise fail or silently misbehave partway through a training run. `underrepresented_labels` catches classes represented so thinly that the fine-tune has little real precedent to learn a class boundary from, echoing the few-shot coverage problem from the prompting module, now checked at dataset-preparation time. `length_range` is a cheap first signal for distribution mismatch -- if production requests are typically several hundred characters and this range tops out at sixty, that's a concrete, checkable early warning that the training distribution likely doesn't match real traffic, worth investigating before spending a training run on it.

misconceptions.description: More training examples is always better, regardless of how carefully they were reviewed -- a bigger dataset can only help, or at worst just be somewhat inefficient.
misconceptions.clarification: Every training example produces a gradient signal that the optimizer trusts equally by default, so a mislabeled or unrepresentative example doesn't sit inertly diluting the dataset -- it actively pushes weights toward the wrong association, with the same confidence as a correct example. Growing a dataset without growing the review effort behind it grows the absolute number of such actively-wrong signals, even if the error rate stays constant, and a smaller, carefully verified dataset routinely outperforms a much larger, less-reviewed one for exactly this reason.

misconceptions.description: As long as training loss is steadily decreasing during a fine-tuning run, the model is learning the intended behavior well.
misconceptions.clarification: A steadily decreasing training loss is consistent with genuine, generalizable learning, but it's equally consistent with the model increasingly memorizing quirks specific to the training examples themselves -- their exact phrasing, their particular format, accidental patterns in how they were constructed -- rather than the broader behavior you actually want. Only performance on a held-out validation split, drawn from a distribution that genuinely matches real usage, can distinguish generalization from memorization; training loss alone, measured only on the data the model is directly being fit to, cannot.

exercises.prompt: This function builds a fine-tuning dataset from a support-ticket database, but the resulting fine-tune ends up giving the exact same canned-sounding response to a common ticket type, ignoring real variation in how those tickets are actually phrased. Find the bug in the dataset-building logic and fix it.
hints: This function takes tickets in whatever order the database happens to return them, and stops as soon as it hits max_examples -- if one common ticket category is heavily overrepresented near the start of that ordering, what ends up dominating the resulting dataset?

Nothing here checks for near-duplicate or highly similar (question, reply) pairs -- if the same common issue produces hundreds of very similar tickets with very similar canned replies, how many effectively-identical examples might end up in the first 5000?

Consider deduplicating near-identical examples and/or capping how many examples any single ticket category can contribute, so the dataset doesn't end up dominated by whichever pattern happened to be most common in the raw ticket volume.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original function has no deduplication and no per-category cap -- it simply takes tickets in whatever order the database returns them until it hits `max_examples`, so if one common issue generates a disproportionate share of all tickets (which is typical -- a handful of issue types usually dominate real support volume), that one category can end up filling most or all of the dataset with highly similar, often near-identical, question/reply pairs. Since gradient descent doesn't discount repeated near-duplicates as 'the same signal counted once' -- it applies the gradient from every example -- an overrepresented category effectively gets its pattern reinforced far more strongly than any other, producing exactly the reported symptom: an inflexible, canned-sounding response to that ticket type and comparatively weak coverage of everything else. The fix adds both a duplicate check (skip prompts already seen) and an explicit per-category cap, so the resulting dataset's category balance reflects a deliberate choice rather than an accident of whatever order and volume the raw ticket data happened to arrive in.

exercises.prompt: Write a function label_balance(examples, min_fraction) that takes a list of dicts each with a "label" key, and returns a dict with two keys: "counts" (a dict mapping each label to how many examples have it) and "underrepresented" (a list of labels whose share of the total is strictly below min_fraction). This is meant to catch classes that are technically present in a dataset but too thin to give the model real precedent to learn from.
hints: Count occurrences of each label first -- a dict or collections.Counter works well here.
A label's "fraction" is its count divided by the total number of examples, not divided by the number of distinct labels.
Compare each label's fraction against min_fraction using a strict less-than -- a label sitting exactly at the threshold should NOT be flagged as underrepresented.
exercises.solutionExplanation: This is a direct, checkable implementation of the coverage principle from the explanation: a class can be technically present in a dataset (here, both 'negative' and 'neutral' genuinely have examples) while still being so thin relative to the whole that the fine-tune has little real signal to learn that class's boundary from. Counting with `Counter` and dividing each count by the total gives each label's actual share of the dataset, which is the number that matters -- not the raw count in isolation, since 5 examples might be plenty in a 20-example dataset but clearly thin in a 10,000-example one. Flagging with strict `<` rather than `<=` means a label sitting exactly at the threshold is treated as acceptable, matching the stated requirement precisely. This kind of check is meant to run before committing to a training run, specifically so a skewed class balance is caught and can be deliberately corrected (through targeted collection or upsampling) rather than discovered only after the fine-tune already underperforms on the underrepresented classes.

assessments.prompt: A team is choosing between fine-tuning on 50,000 examples scraped automatically from old support logs with an estimated 8% mislabeling rate, or 2,000 examples that were individually hand-verified for correct labels. Which is more likely to produce a better fine-tune, and why?
options: The 50,000-example set, because fine-tuning quality is primarily a function of dataset size, and a mislabeling rate under 10% is negligible at that scale.

The 2,000-example set, because mislabeled examples actively teach the wrong association rather than merely diluting the signal, and 8% of 50,000 is a large, systematic amount of actively-wrong training signal.
They are roughly equivalent, since gradient descent naturally discounts a small minority of incorrect examples during training regardless of dataset size.
The 50,000-example set, because a larger validation split can always be carved out of it afterward to compensate for the mislabeling.
assessments.explanation: Gradient descent trusts every labeled example equally by default -- there's no built-in mechanism that automatically discounts examples just because they're a minority of the dataset, which is exactly what option C incorrectly assumes. 8% of 50,000 examples is 4,000 actively mislabeled training signals, each pushing weights toward an incorrect association with the same confidence as a correct example; that's a substantial, not negligible, source of wrong signal, contradicting option A. Option D misunderstands what a validation split is for -- carving one out of the same noisy dataset doesn't remove the noisy examples still used for training, and a validation split drawn from an equally noisy source wouldn't reliably reveal the problem anyway. The hand-verified, smaller dataset avoids this actively-wrong signal almost entirely, which is why it's the stronger choice despite being 25 times smaller.

assessments.prompt: Explain, mechanically in terms of gradient updates, why a fine-tuning dataset with a nontrivial fraction of mislabeled examples doesn't just 'partially help' the fine-tune -- it can make the model measurably worse at the task than not fine-tuning at all. Also explain what role a held-out validation set plays in catching this before it ships.
assessments.modelAnswer: Every training example, correct or not, produces a gradient during backpropagation -- a specific, calculated direction and magnitude that the optimizer uses to nudge every trainable weight, with the explicit goal of making the model assign higher probability to that example's target completion given its input. The optimizer has no independent way to tell a correctly-labeled example from a mislabeled one; both are treated as equally trustworthy ground truth by default, and both produce a gradient applied with identical confidence. This means a mislabeled example isn't neutral or 'wasted' -- it actively teaches the model that, given an input like this one, the correct-sounding response looks like the (actually wrong) target it was paired with. A single isolated mislabel among thousands of correct examples might have a negligible net effect, since its individual gradient signal is small relative to everything else pulling in the right direction. But a *systematic* fraction of mislabeled examples -- the same kind of error repeated across many examples, as opposed to scattered, independent noise -- is a consistent, correlated signal that gradient descent is specifically good at learning, just pointed at the wrong target; enough of that correlated wrong-signal can outweigh the correct signal on exactly the inputs it affects, producing a fine-tuned model that's measurably worse on that slice of the task than the original, untouched base model would have been, precisely because it was actively taught the wrong association rather than merely left un-improved. A held-out validation set -- crucially, one that's itself been verified as accurately labeled, and drawn from a distribution that matches real usage -- is what catches this before deployment: since the mislabeling problem lives specifically in what the training set is teaching the model to output, checking performance against a clean, independent reference set that wasn't used for training is what reveals a gap between 'looks good because the model was fit to match this exact (flawed) data' and 'actually good at the underlying task,' a gap that watching training loss decrease on the flawed training set alone can never reveal, since training loss is measuring exactly the thing the flawed labels were used to define as correct.

assessments.prompt: Per this module, why can a model fine-tuned exclusively on bare prompt/completion pairs (no system prompt, no retrieved context, no conversation history) underperform in production even if every individual training label is correctly written?
options: Bare prompt/completion pairs are always rejected outright by fine-tuning APIs, so this scenario could not actually occur in practice.
