The model was trained on a mapping from an input shape it will essentially never see in production, since real requests include a system prompt, injected context, and history -- and there's no guarantee that what it learned from the clean, minimal training format transfers cleanly to that messier, fuller real request shape.
Bare prompt/completion pairs always take substantially longer to tokenize, which measurably slows down the model's convergence during training.
Fine-tuning APIs silently discard any training example that lacks an explicit system message before training begins.
assessments.explanation: The module ties this directly to format fidelity: training data teaches a mapping from a specific input shape to a desired output shape, and if that trained-on shape doesn't match what real requests actually look like, nothing guarantees the learned behavior transfers cleanly -- even though every individual label might be perfectly correct in isolation. Option A invents an API restriction the module never mentions. Option C attributes the problem to tokenization speed, an unrelated concern. Option D invents a silent-discard behavior that isn't part of how fine-tuning APIs are described as working.

assessments.prompt: Per this module, why can training loss keep decreasing steadily throughout a fine-tuning run even as the model increasingly just memorizes quirks specific to the training examples rather than learning behavior that generalizes?
options: Training loss is measured only against the training data itself, so by construction it cannot distinguish genuine generalization from memorization of that same data -- only a held-out validation split drawn from a representative distribution can reveal that difference.
Training loss is effectively a random number generated independently of the model's actual weight values, so it carries no real information either way.
Training loss always rises sharply the moment memorization begins, so a steadily decreasing loss is, by itself, proof that memorization is not occurring.
Memorization is mathematically impossible under gradient descent, so this described scenario could not actually happen in a real training run.
assessments.explanation: The module states this precisely: a steadily dropping training loss is consistent with genuine learning and with pure memorization alike, because it's only ever checked against the same data the model is being fit to -- which is exactly why a held-out validation split from a representative distribution is necessary to actually tell the two apart. Option B mischaracterizes training loss as meaningless noise, contradicting its real, direct relationship to the model's fit on the training data. Option C asserts the opposite of the module's point -- decreasing loss is explicitly described as compatible with memorization, not evidence against it. Option D denies a phenomenon the module treats as a real, common risk.

assessments.prompt: A support-ticket training dataset is built by pulling examples in raw database order until a fixed example count is reached, with no deduplication and no per-category cap. Per this module, what's the likely consequence, and why?
options: No real consequence -- database order has no bearing on dataset composition, since every ticket is equally likely to be included regardless of order.

Whichever ticket category is most common in raw volume is likely to dominate the resulting dataset with many near-identical examples, and since gradient descent applies a gradient to every example rather than discounting repeated near-duplicates, that category's pattern gets disproportionately reinforced at the expense of others.
The dataset will automatically balance itself, since fine-tuning APIs enforce a hard cap on how many similar examples can be drawn from any single source category.
This concern only applies to classification-style tasks and has no relevance to tasks involving generated free-text replies like support-ticket responses.
assessments.explanation: The module's own debugging exercise describes exactly this setup and diagnosis: an unordered pull with no dedup and no per-category cap tends to let whichever category is most common in raw volume dominate the resulting dataset, and because gradient descent doesn't discount repeated near-duplicates as one signal counted once, that overrepresented category's pattern gets reinforced far more strongly than others. Option A ignores that real-world ticket categories are rarely uniformly distributed in raw order or volume. Option C invents an automatic safeguard that fine-tuning APIs don't provide. Option D incorrectly limits the concern to classification, when the module's own example is specifically about free-text support replies.
